intro_html:
In New York today, a balcony panel that feeds a household circuit is treated like any other generator. Con Edison asks anyone installing distributed generation to complete an interconnection application in its PowerClerk portal before installing, a process built for permanent systems. The SUNNY Act would replace that, for devices of up to 1,200 W AC, with a simple form sent to the utility within 30 days of installation. It has passed both chambers and {{sunny.phrase}}; if signed, it takes effect 90 days later.

Two details decide how much it would change for an apartment. The bill requires a device to be listed or certified by an accredited laboratory as a complete plug-in system, and as of August 2026 no kit had been certified as a complete system under UL 3700, the standard written for that purpose. And it has no landlord, co-op, condominium or local-government provision, so a lease, a proprietary lease or a condo board’s rules on railings and facades would still decide whether a panel goes up. Exported power would be unpaid unless the customer signs a net-metering or other compensation agreement.

For New York City addresses, balco.nyc’s calculator models shade from surrounding buildings in 3D and values each kWh at Con Edison’s marginal rate of about {{coned.rate_cents}}¢, not the statewide average used elsewhere on this page. Where the SUNNY Act stands.

faq: Can I use a balcony solar panel in New York City before the SUNNY Act is signed?

Only through Con Edison's interconnection process, which asks anyone installing distributed generation to apply through its PowerClerk portal before installing and was built for permanent systems. The SUNNY Act (S8512C / A9111C) would exempt plug-in devices of up to 1,200 W AC; it has passed both chambers and {{sunny.phrase}}.
